The Long Road to a Dissertation: 校园生活
从选题、导师会谈到查重与答辩,一篇毕业论文如何把三年的阅读变成一项独立研究。
B2

The dissertation looms over every final-year student, and mine was no exception. It began not with a burst of inspiration but with a spreadsheet: three columns labelled "idea", "sources", and "can I actually finish this?" My supervisor, a patient woman who had read more lukewarm drafts than she could count, told me during our first meeting that a good project is narrow enough to answer and wide enough to matter. I pitched five topics. She killed four of them in ten minutes, and the survivor — how first-year students learn to reference honestly — became my companion for the next eight months.

The early weeks were deceptively pleasant. I sat in the library reading everything I could find, filling notebooks with summaries and feeling productive. My supervisor soon corrected that illusion. Reading, she said, is not research; research is deciding what the reading means. She sent me back with one instruction: turn every note into a claim, and attach a citation to every claim. That single piece of advice transformed my work. Suddenly the pile of articles was not an obstacle but a conversation, and my job was to say something new within it.

The middle months tested my honesty. Writing about referencing meant wrestling with plagiarism in its greyest forms — the paraphrase that clings too closely to the original, the borrowed phrase that slips in without quotation marks, the source half-remembered and cited from memory. None of these feel like cheating to a nervous eighteen-year-old; they feel like shortcuts invented under pressure, which is precisely why they survive so long unnoticed. I interviewed twelve first-years about how they had been taught to handle sources, sitting with each one for half an hour while they talked me through a real essay they had written. Their candour surprised me. One admitted she had cited a book she never opened, purely because the reading list made it look impressive; another confessed to copying two sentences word for word the night before a deadline, then lying awake certain he would be caught. Most wanted to do the right thing; few had ever been shown how. Their confusion became the heart of my argument: universities punish what they never properly teach, and the gap between expectation and instruction is where good students quietly go wrong.

Then came the silent disaster of the data chapter. Half of my interview recordings were corrupted by a faulty app, and for one grey Tuesday I genuinely believed the project was over. The rescue came from an unexpected quarter: the coursework skills I had complained about for two years. I had transcripts for six interviews, enough notes to reconstruct four more, and a supervisor who insisted that a smaller, deeper sample would strengthen rather than weaken the chapter. She was right. The revised argument was sharper because it had to be.

The final month was pure carpentry: shaping chapters, cutting repetition, formatting the bibliography until every full stop obeyed the style guide. There is a peculiar loneliness in that stage; the interviews are over, the seminars have ended, and the dissertation exists nowhere except on your screen and in your supervisor's marginal comments. I gave myself a production line: two hundred words before breakfast, one completed section each week, a printed draft carried to the same café every Friday for a cold read. I learned that deadline pressure is not the enemy of good writing; structure is its shelter. Because each chapter had been argued and evidenced as I went, the ending arrived on schedule — a sensation my younger self, who once wrote an entire coursework essay in one panicky night, would have found unbelievable.

The viva, when it finally came, lasted fifty minutes and felt like the most concentrated seminar of my life. Two examiners, neither of whom I had met, asked me to defend my choices: why this method, why these students, what I would do differently. The moment I stopped performing and started thinking aloud, the room warmed. Walking out into the corridor, still clutching my own battered copy, I understood what the dissertation had really taught me: not a topic, but the discipline of turning curiosity into evidence, one honest sentence at a time — and the quiet confidence that, given a year and a library card, I could do it again.
